Bodt 2018 note (5 pp.): p. 1 (rhythm; 'clearly pronounce a short, unstressed initial syllable'); p. 2 section 'Constricted syllables always unstressed' (fixed: second syllable statement incl. suffixes); pp. 3-4 Table 1 and p. 5 Table 4 (Khoitam Sartang cognates transcribed with root stress); p. 4 'prefixes remaining unstressed' and 'the root always carried the stress, a situation that is reflected in the comtemporary Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties'.
catalog_quote: [Bodt 2024 p. 156] Whereas in Khispi and Duhumbi the meter in most words consists of a stressed syllable followed by one or more unstressed syllables, in the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties an unstressed syllable is followed by a stressed syllable, in other words, the Khispi and Duhumbi rhythm is trochaic, that of the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties iambic. ... In iambic languages, the first syllable of a word is unstressed and most commonly short, whereas the second syllable is stressed, and longer. [pp. 170-171] The Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties, on the other hand, obtained iambic rhythm through language contact, stressing the second syllable of a word, which, in the case of prefixed words, is always the root and not the prefix. Because of the lack of stress on the prefix, the prefix loses its vowel, either by replacement with a shwa or by complete elision. [p. 301, §50c] The short vowel rhymes are conditioned by a lack of stress on these suffixes. [Bodt 2018 p. 2] ... the closest genetic relatives Sartang and Sherdukpen ... follow an iambic foot, with stress always on the second syllable of a bisyllabic word, whether that is the root preceded by an unstressed prefix, or a suffix preceded by an unstressed root. [Bodt 2018 p. 4] In Proto-Western Kho-Bwa, prefixes are presumed to have never been stressed, whereas the root always carried the stress, a situation that is reflected in the comtemporary Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and re-extracted the cited pages with extracted text/-l. Page numbers sit at the foot of each page; p. 177 = printed p. 156 and carries the heading '4.2 Iambic versus trochaic rhythm' and the first quoted sentence exactly as reported: 'Whereas in Khispi and Duhumbi the meter in most words consists of a stressed syllable followed by one or more unstressed syllables, in the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties an unstressed syllable is followed by a stressed syllable, in other words, the Khispi and Duhumbi rhythm is trochaic, that of the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties iambic.' The same page adds: 'In iambic languages, the first syllable of a word is unstressed and most commonly short, wh…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sartang words are iambic: the typical inherited word is (prefix +) root (+ suffix); the prefix / minor first syllable is unstressed, short, reduced to Cə- or a bare consonant (giving the apparent onset clusters), and stress falls on the root, which in prefixed words is the second syllable; grammatical suffixes are unstressed (p. 300: their short rhymes are 'conditioned by a lack of stress on these suffixes'). So stress sits on the lexical root = second/last full syllable of the prosodic stem; could alternatively be filed as fixed: second syllable (iambic) for prefix+root words.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'in most words'. Prefix reduction is uneven: in allegro speech prefixes are Ci-, in careful/elicited speech Ciə-, and when speakers slow down an echo vowel appears (Khoitam [slyŋ] ~ [sə.lyŋ] ~ [sy.lyŋ] 'heart'); a few items keep a full-vowel prefix (Khoina 'mud', 'amaranth'; Khoitam 'amaranth'), which Bodt takes to mean the trochaic > iambic shift is recent and 'has not yet progressed evenly in all varieties and all phonotactic environments'. Compounds, trisyllabic words and loans are not covered by the statement. No tone; the varieties have short glottal-constricted vowels with rising pitch versus long modal/breathy vowels (secs 3.3-3.6), described as a vowel contrast rather than tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rhythm/stress of the morphological word, stated for elicited lexical items (citation forms) and allegro speech alike; the statement is made jointly for 'the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties' in a comparative-historical monograph (no dedicated Sartang prosody section), but rests on the author's own 2012-2019 fieldwork on all four Sartang varieties (Khoina, Jerigaon, Khoitam, Rahung). Same claim, first-hand, in Bodt's 2018 Zenodo note (10.5281/zenodo.1284482): 'the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties have iambic, not trochaic rhythm.. the second, stressed syllable (the root)'.
new_statements.identity_note: Bodt 2024's 'Sartang varieties' are Khoina, Jerigaon, Khoitam and Rahung — i.e. the whole of sart1249 (Glottolog lists no dialects; Dondrup 2004's 'Boot Monpa' = the same language, spoken in Khoitam, Rahung, Salari, Jerigaon and Khoina per Wikipedia citing Dondrup 2004:1). The stress statement is framed jointly for the Sartang and the Sherdukpen varieties Rupa and Shergaon (sher1257), which Bodt treats as one dialect continuum; the same wording therefore already backs the sher1257 entry, and Sartang inherits it as the second language of the pair, not as an independent description.

sources.citation: Bodt, Timotheus Adrianus. 2018. Duhumbi Phonology - Iambic to Trochaic Rhythm? Zenodo, 4 pp. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1284482.
sources.note: p. 1: 'the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties have iambic, not trochaic rhythm.. The initial, unstressed syllable is short and usually ending on an open vowel, whereas the second, stressed syllable (the root) has a fully formed syllable'; the unstressed initial syllable is a-, sə-, kə-, bə- etc., often a prefix; speakers 'when lexemes are elicited in isolation, clearly pronounce a short, unstressed initial syllable, even though in allegro speech this is realised as a cluster'.
Nothing; distribution and varieties only (cites Dondrup 2004:1 for villages Khoitam, Rahung, Namku-thangka/Salari, Boot/Jerigaon, Khoina; Blench 2015; Lieberherr & Bodt 2017).
